summary:
**Division O — Other Matters** is not a normal department funding bill. It is a catch-all package of policy changes attached to the FY2016 omnibus (H.R. 2029). It covers oil exports, travel security, 9/11 health and compensation, Medicare and Medicaid payment rules, Puerto Rico hospitals, financial regulation, conservation, oceans, budget scorekeeping, and a loan program for Iraq.

## Overview

This division does not fund one federal department. It bundles unrelated laws that change energy policy, border and visa rules, long-term benefits for people harmed by the September 11 attacks and by state-sponsored terrorism, health-program payments, housing programs left over from the financial crisis, and a few conservation and foreign-aid authorities.

## Total Spending

No single total is stated, and one cannot be added up cleanly. The division mixes new appropriations, a large rescission, spending caps, multi-year mandatory fund deposits, authorizations (permission to spend later), and loan authority.

The clearest new money in the text is:

- **$4.6 billion** appropriated for fiscal year 2017 for newer September 11th Victim Compensation Fund claims, available until spent.
- **$1.025 billion** appropriated for fiscal year 2017 for a new fund for U.S. victims of state-sponsored terrorism, available until spent.
- **$3.8 billion** permanently canceled from money the government received in the BNP Paribas settlement and held in a Treasury forfeiture fund.

Those three items do not net to a simple “cost of the division,” because other provisions add or cut spending over many years without a combined total.

## Key Funding Areas

- **September 11th Victim Compensation Fund (newer “Group B” claims)**: $4.6 billion for fiscal year 2017 — pays compensation for eligible 9/11-related physical injuries and deaths under tightened rules; available until spent.
- **U.S. Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund**: $1.025 billion for fiscal year 2017 — pays eligible Americans who won terrorism-related court judgments, plus set amounts for Iran hostage-crisis victims and certain family members; available until spent, with new obligations barred after January 2, 2026.
- **World Trade Center Health Program**: specified federal deposits of $330 million in fiscal year 2016, rising each year to $570 million in fiscal year 2025, then adjusted for inflation through fiscal year 2090 — medical monitoring and treatment for eligible 9/11 responders and survivors. Smaller set-asides in the text include $15 million for fiscal year 2017 for one program activity and $750,000 a year for another.
- **Earlier 9/11 compensation claims (“Group A”)**: capped at $2.775 billion in federal funds — finishes payments on claims that already had a final award, including amounts previously reduced because the old cap ran short. This is a cap, not a new appropriation stated in this section.
- **BNP Paribas settlement funds**: $3.8 billion rescinded — cancels that amount in the Treasury Forfeiture Fund and bars the Justice Department from using the BNP settlement the way it had proposed on May 1, 2015. Congress instead routes victim compensation through the funds created in this division.
- **Iraq defense loans**: up to $2.7 billion in principal in fiscal year 2016 — government-backed loans to buy U.S. defense articles and services, repayable within 12 years. This is loan authority, not a $2.7 billion grant. Subsidy costs come from Foreign Military Financing funds already designated for overseas contingency operations, and those funds cannot pay Iraq’s loan fees.
- **Hardest Hit Fund**: up to $2 billion more may be obligated, and authority may run through December 31, 2017 — only for housing agencies already in the program for the hardest-hit housing markets. This extends existing crisis-era authority; it is not written as a new general-fund appropriation.
- **Maritime Security Program**: authorizes about $300 million a year — $299,997,000 in fiscal year 2017, $300 million in each of fiscal years 2018–2020, and $314,007,780 in fiscal year 2021 — for payments to U.S.-flag commercial ships that must be available for national defense. Per-ship payments are set near $5 million. These are authorizations, not appropriations in this division.
- **Medicare Improvement Fund**: cut from $205 million to $5 million — a $200 million reduction in a Medicare reserve account, not new spending.
- **9/11 Response and Biometric Exit Account**: funded by higher visa fees, not a stated appropriation — certain large employers pay an extra $4,500 on L-1 visa applications and an extra $4,000 on H-1B applications through September 30, 2025. Half of that extra fee goes to this account until deposits reach $1 billion; the other half goes to the general Treasury. After $1 billion is deposited, all of the extra fees go to the Treasury.

## Notable Provisions

- **Crude oil exports**: Repeals the old export-restriction law and bars federal officials from restricting U.S. crude oil exports. The President can still block exports under sanctions, emergencies, and similar laws, and can reimpose limits for up to one year at a time if exports cause serious supply shortages, prices far above world levels, and lasting job losses.
- **Visa Waiver Program**: Starting April 1, 2016, travelers need an electronic passport with biometric data. People who were in Iraq or Syria on or after March 1, 2011, who traveled to other terrorism-sponsor countries or areas DHS designates, or who are nationals of those places, generally cannot use visa-free entry. Exceptions cover some military and government duty, and DHS may waive the rule for law-enforcement or national-security reasons. Partner countries must report lost or stolen passports within 24 hours, screen travelers against Interpol where required, and share passenger information or risk losing visa-waiver status.
- **9/11 health program**: Extended through October 1, 2090, with authority to add health conditions after scientific review and outside peer review. Enrollment cutoffs that had run through fiscal year 2020 are removed.
- **9/11 compensation fund**: Reopened for five years after regulations are updated. Newer claims generally require a certified World Trade Center-related physical condition. Mental-health conditions alone do not qualify for this compensation. For newer claims, noneconomic awards are capped at $250,000 for cancer and $90,000 for other conditions, and annual earnings counted toward economic loss are capped at $200,000. The Manhattan exposure zone is redefined using Canal Street, East Broadway, and Clinton Street.
- **State-sponsored terrorism victims**: Creates a special master and a fund paid from the $1.025 billion appropriation plus certain penalties and forfeitures tied to state sponsors of terrorism. Iran embassy hostages (November 4, 1979–January 20, 1981) are eligible for $10,000 per day held; each eligible spouse or child in the named court case gets a $600,000 lump sum. Individual claims are treated as no more than $20 million for payment purposes, and a person plus immediate family is capped at $35 million combined. Payments are pro rata until everyone is paid. Attorney fees are capped at 25 percent. Someone criminally responsible for the terrorist act cannot be paid.
- **Sequestration protection**: The 9/11 victim fund, the World Trade Center Health Program Fund, and the state-sponsored terrorism victims fund are added to the list of programs exempt from automatic spending cuts.
- **Medicare imaging**: Starting in 2017, Medicare pays 20 percent less for the technical side of film X-rays. Cassette-based “computed radiography” is cut 7 percent from 2018 through 2022 and 10 percent after that, in both physician and hospital-outpatient payments. The professional-fee discount when multiple imaging services are done together drops from 25 percent to 5 percent starting in 2017.
- **Medicaid equipment**: Beginning January 1, 2019, federal Medicaid payments to states for durable medical equipment cannot exceed what Medicare would pay in total for each class of items. States may still cover equipment Medicare does not cover.
- **Home health devices**: Starting January 1, 2017, Medicare pays separately for certain disposable negative-pressure wound-therapy systems used in home health, at 80 percent of the applicable outpatient rate. Patients owe the usual coinsurance.
- **Puerto Rico hospitals**: Starting January 1, 2016, Medicare inpatient payments use the full federal rate rather than a blended Puerto Rico rate. Puerto Rico hospitals are also brought into Medicare electronic-health-record incentive payments, with deadlines shifted later to account for the delay.
- **Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac**: Treasury may not sell or otherwise dispose of its senior preferred stock in the two companies before at least January 1, 2018, unless a new law specifically tells it to. Congress says it should pass legislation on their future and that Treasury should not sell even after that date until such a law exists. That second point is a statement of congressional opinion, not a binding ban.
- **Financial rules**: Narrows when corporate affiliates can use the Dodd-Frank exemption from mandatory swap clearing. Requires Consumer Financial Protection Bureau advisory committees to follow the Federal Advisory Committee Act. Limits federal “source of strength” demands on insurance companies that own banks, and requires notice to state insurance regulators before certain liens in a liquidation. Bars SEC funds in this Act from being used to finish or carry out rules requiring disclosure of political contributions, donations to tax-exempt groups, or trade-association dues.
- **Housing programs**: Making Home Affordable, including new applications, ends December 31, 2016. Applications already filed under the Home Affordable Modification Program by that date can continue.
- **Land and Water Conservation Fund**: The fund’s authorization, which had been set to end September 30, 2015, is extended through September 30, 2018. This section does not state a dollar amount. For fiscal years 2016–2018, land-acquisition money generally cannot be used to file condemnation cases without approval from the House and Senate Appropriations Committees, except for specified Everglades acquisition and restoration.
- **Oceans and coasts**: Creates a National Oceans and Coastal Security Fund, to be run with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, for research, ocean observing, coastal resources, and coastal infrastructure. Congress authorizes “such sums as are necessary” for fiscal years 2017–2019; no dollar amount is set. Administrative costs are capped at 2 percent. Money cannot fund lawsuits against the federal government or the creation of national marine monuments, marine protected areas, marine spatial planning, or the National Ocean Policy. Foreign-government donations are barred.
- **Budget rules**: Divisions of the bill starting with Division M are kept off statutory and Senate pay-as-you-go scorecards. The House Budget Committee chair may adjust fiscal year 2016 budget allocations to match the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015.

## Who Benefits

- **9/11 responders, survivors, and families** with covered physical illnesses, through health coverage into 2090 and additional compensation money.
- **Americans with terrorism-related court judgments**, and former Iran embassy hostages and certain spouses and children.
- **U.S. oil producers and exporters**, who gain a general right to export crude oil, subject to emergency and sanctions exceptions.
- **U.S.-flag ship operators** in the Maritime Security Program, if later appropriations match the new authorization.
- **Puerto Rico hospitals**, through higher Medicare inpatient rates and access to electronic-health-record incentive payments.
- **Home-health patients using a specified disposable wound-therapy device**, and imaging providers who move from film to digital systems; film and older cassette-based X-ray payments go down.
- **States and coastal communities**, if oceans money is later appropriated, and land-conservation programs through the extended conservation-fund authorization.
- **Housing agencies already in the Hardest Hit Fund**, for a limited additional period.
- **Iraq**, through up to $2.7 billion in defense-purchase loans, with special emphasis, in consultation with Iraq, on groups defined as “covered groups” in a 2015 defense law.
- **Federal security agencies and the traveling public**, through tighter visa-waiver screening. Some travelers who previously entered without a visa will instead need a visa.

People and institutions that lose ground under the text include film X-ray providers, state Medicaid programs that paid more than Medicare for equipment, employers that rely heavily on H-1B and L-1 workers, and the Justice Department’s previously announced use of the BNP settlement.

## Plain English Summary

This is the “everything else” chapter of the big 2016 spending bill. It lifts the long-standing ban on shipping American crude oil overseas, with a safety valve if that causes real shortages and job losses. It makes visa-free travel harder for people who have been in Iraq, Syria, or other terrorism-linked places, and it requires tougher passports and screening from partner countries. The largest new checks are for September 11 health care and compensation — health coverage is extended all the way to 2090, and about $4.6 billion is set aside for newer victim claims — plus about $1 billion for Americans hurt by state-sponsored terrorism, paid for in part by canceling $3.8 billion from a bank settlement fund. It also trims some Medicare and Medicaid payments, raises what Medicare pays Puerto Rico hospitals, freezes any sale of the government’s Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac stock until at least 2018, keeps a shrinking housing-aid program alive a bit longer, and allows Iraq to borrow up to $2.7 billion to buy American military equipment.

titles.header: OIL EXPORTS, SAFETY VALVE, AND MARITIME SECURITY
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

Title I repeals the longstanding statutory restriction on exporting U.S. crude oil and bars federal officials from imposing or enforcing crude-oil export limits, subject to emergency, sanctions, and a temporary “safety valve.” It does not appropriate funds to an energy agency. It also raises statutory payment rates and authorization levels for the Maritime Security Program (MSP), which pays U.S.-flag commercial ships to remain available for national defense sealift.

## Spending Breakdown

These figures amend permanent law (46 U.S.C. §§ 53106 and 53111). They are per-vessel payment rates and authorizations of appropriations, not new appropriations enacted in this title. The totals match a 60-ship fleet.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| MSP payment per vessel, FY2017 | $4,999,950 | Annual stipend for each enrolled U.S.-flag vessel |
| MSP payment per vessel, FY2018, FY2019, and FY2020 | $5,000,000 each year | Same, for each of those three years |
| MSP payment per vessel, FY2021 | $5,233,463 | Same, for FY2021 |
| MSP authorization of appropriations, FY2017 | $299,997,000 | Total amount authorized for the program |
| MSP authorization of appropriations, FY2018, FY2019, and FY2020 | $300,000,000 each year | Total amount authorized for each of those years |
| MSP authorization of appropriations, FY2021 | $314,007,780 | Total amount authorized for FY2021 |

## Notable Sections

- **SEC. 101(a)–(b) — Export-ban repeal.** Repeals section 103 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (42 U.S.C. 6212) and states that, except as provided in subsections (c) and (d), no federal official may impose or enforce any restriction on crude-oil exports.
- **SEC. 101(c) — Savings clause.** Preserves the President’s authority under the Constitution, IEEPA, the National Emergencies Act, EPCA emergency authorities, the Trading With the Enemy Act, and other sanctions laws (including restrictions involving state sponsors of terrorism). It carves out 15 C.F.R. § 754.2, the regulation that implemented the export licensing regime.
- **SEC. 101(d) — Safety valve.** Allows the President to impose export licensing or other restrictions for up to one year (renewable in one-year increments if based on a declared national emergency) if: a national emergency is declared and noticed in the Federal Register; restrictions are tied to national-security sanctions or trade limits; or Commerce, with Energy, finds that U.S. crude exports have caused sustained material supply shortages or prices well above world levels, with sustained material adverse U.S. employment effects.
- **SEC. 101(e) — Maritime Security Program.** Resets MSP per-ship payments and the program’s authorization through FY2021 at the amounts in the table above.

## Plain English

This title ends the general ban on shipping U.S. crude oil overseas, while leaving emergency and sanctions powers in place, and increases federal payments that keep a fleet of U.S.-flag cargo ships ready for military sealift.

titles.header: TERRORIST TRAVEL PREVENTION AND VISA WAIVER PROGRAM REFORM
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

Title II enacts the Visa Waiver Program Improvement and Terrorist Travel Prevention Act of 2015. It amends the Visa Waiver Program in the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1187), tightening who may enter the United States without a visa and what participating countries must do on passports, screening, and information sharing. The title sets duties for the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of State, and the Director of National Intelligence; it does not appropriate funds.

## Spending Breakdown

This title contains **no appropriations and no dollar amounts**. Section 208 directs risk-based assistance to non-program countries but does not authorize or specify a sum.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| All sections (201–210) | No amount specified | Policy amendments to the Visa Waiver Program; no funding provided in this title |
| Sec. 208 (assistance to non-program countries) | No amount specified | Directs DHS, with the State Department, to help non-participating countries report lost or stolen passports to Interpol and issue and validate electronic passports |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 202 — Electronic passports.** Beginning April 1, 2016, Visa Waiver travelers must hold an electronic passport with biographic and biometric data. By October 1, 2016, program countries must certify they can validate those passports at key ports of entry (Schengen-zone travel is exempt). Repeals 8 U.S.C. 1732(c).
- **Sec. 203 — Travel and nationality bar.** Bars Visa Waiver use for people present on or after March 1, 2011, in Iraq, Syria, a designated state sponsor of terrorism, or another country or area of concern named by the Secretary of Homeland Security—and for nationals of those places, including dual nationals of a program country. Military and full-time government employees of program countries are excepted for presence; the Secretary may waive the bar for law enforcement or national security reasons and must report each waiver to Congress. Additional countries or areas must be considered within 60 days and reviewed annually.
- **Sec. 204 — Country obligations and termination.** Lost or stolen passports must be reported within 24 hours. Within 270 days, program countries (except those without an international airport, and except Schengen travel) must screen non-citizens entering or leaving against Interpol databases. Failure to share passenger information or to screen requires termination of program status, with redesignation only after compliance.
- **Sec. 206 — High-risk countries.** Requires an annual security evaluation (including travel to Iraq or Syria to engage in terrorism, terrorist-database hits, passport fraud, and border control) and allows suspension of a country’s designation. A threat report is due within 60 days and then annually.
- **Sec. 207 — ESTA changes.** Lets DHS shorten travel-authorization validity, requires collection of additional or prior citizenships, and requires fraud-detection research plus reports on denials and revocations.
- **Sec. 210 — Sense of Congress.** Urges the International Civil Aviation Organization to set electronic-passport standards and require member countries to use them. Non-binding.

## Plain English

People from visa-waiver countries can still visit the United States without a visa only if they have a modern electronic passport and have not traveled to, or hold nationality of, Iraq, Syria, or certain other terrorism-related countries, unless Homeland Security grants a waiver.

titles.header: JAMES ZADROGA 9/11 HEALTH AND COMPENSATION REAUTHORIZATION ACT
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

This title is the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Reauthorization Act. The text provided (Secs. 301–302) reauthorizes the World Trade Center Health Program under the Public Health Service Act and sets mandatory federal deposits into the World Trade Center Health Program Fund for fiscal years 2016 through 2090. It covers monitoring and treatment for enrolled WTC responders and survivors, Clinical Centers of Excellence and Data Centers, the WTC Health Registry, education and outreach, and related program administration, with oversight by the WTC Program Administrator and the Government Accountability Office.

## Spending Breakdown

These are federal deposits into the Fund (the federal share), not annual discretionary appropriations. Amounts remain available until expended through FY 2090. Unspent amounts already identified for the Fund under prior law stay in the Fund.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| WTC Health Program Fund, federal share, FY 2016 | $330,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2017 | $345,610,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2018 | $380,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2019 | $440,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2020 | $485,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2021 | $501,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2022 | $518,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2023 | $535,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2024 | $552,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2025 | $570,000,000 | Federal deposit for program costs |
| Federal share, FY 2026–FY 2090 | Prior-year amount plus CPI-U | Annual inflation adjustment (all items; U.S. city average), estimated by the Secretary for the 12 months ending the previous March |

**Specified fixed deposits, FY 2016–FY 2025:** $4,656,610,000, plus CPI-adjusted deposits through FY 2090.

Separate **spending limits inside the Fund** (not extra money on top of the deposits):

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Fund limitation, §3351(c)(2), FY 2016 | $200,000 | Cap on that statutory category for FY 2016; later years follow the redesignated formula |
| Education and outreach (PHS Act §3303) | $750,000 per year | Cap for FY 2016 and each later fiscal year |
| Fund limitation, §3351(c)(4), FY 2017 | $15,000,000 | Cap for FY 2017; FY 2016 continues the pre-enactment determination |
| Other §3351(c) caps for FY 2016 | Prior-law amounts | Several FY 2016 limits keep the amount already set under former subparagraph (C), rather than a new figure in this title |

## Notable Sections

- **Program life extended to 2090.** The Fund is authorized from FY 2016 through FY 2090, and the WTC Program terminates on October 1, 2090. Claim-payment authority is likewise extended through FY 2090.
- **Enrollment sunsets removed.** Language limiting certain responder (§3311) and survivor (§3321) provisions “through the end of fiscal year 2020” is struck.
- **New conditions face more process.** Time for the Administrator and Advisory Committee to act on adding a covered health condition rises from 60 to 90 days. A final rule adding a condition now requires an independent peer review of the scientific and technical evidence. The Advisory Committee must review the policies used to decide whether evidence is sufficient, and must recommend peer reviewers.
- **GAO oversight.** An initial report is due within 18 months on quality assurance, certification of WTC-related conditions, and payment integrity (including workers’ compensation and other coverage, and coordination of benefits). Further assessments run about every five years through FY 2042.
- **Other program changes.** Clinical Centers of Excellence must do outreach **and retention**. The WTC Health Registry reference date moves from April 20, 2009, to January 1, 2015. The Administrator may issue regulations needed to run the title. The Fund’s allowable uses are expanded to a longer list of PHS Act sections, including research, education, data centers, and the registry.

The short title refers to health **and compensation** reauthorization; the sections supplied here address the health program only.

## Plain English

This title locks in federal funding so people made ill by the 9/11 attacks can keep getting monitoring and treatment for decades, with the program set to run until 2090.

titles.header: JAMES ZADROGA 9/11 VICTIM COMPENSATION FUND REAUTHORIZATION
titles.summary:
## Title Summary

This title reauthorizes the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund, extends the claim-filing window, and appropriates new money for later (“Group B”) claims by people with World Trade Center–related physical illnesses, including those tied to rescue and recovery work. It also creates the United States Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund, raises certain H-1B and L-1 visa fees, and rescinds a large share of the BNP Paribas settlement sitting in the Treasury Forfeiture Fund.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Victims Compensation Fund — Group B claims | $4,600,000,000 (FY2017, available until expended) | New appropriation for compensation of Group B 9/11 claims |
| Group A compensation cap | $2,775,000,000 (limit, not a new appropriation) | Ceiling on federal payments for claims that already had a final award determination; unpaid remainder of previously reduced awards must be paid |
| United States Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund | $1,025,000,000 (FY2017, available until expended) | Direct appropriation to pay eligible U.S. persons with judgments or specified hostage claims against state sponsors of terrorism |
| Treasury Forfeiture Fund rescission (BNP Paribas) | $3,800,000,000 permanently rescinded | Removes that amount of the June 27, 2014 BNP Paribas plea-related funds from the Treasury Forfeiture Fund |
| L-1 visa fee increase | +$4,500 per application (through Sept. 30, 2025) | Extra combined filing/fraud fee for certain employers with 50+ U.S. employees if more than 50% are H-1B or L nonimmigrants |
| H-1B visa fee increase | +$4,000 per application (through Sept. 30, 2025) | Same employer test; 50% of collections to the general fund and 50% to the 9–11 Response and Biometric Exit Account until $1,000,000,000 is deposited there, then 100% to the general fund |
| Group B noneconomic-loss caps | $250,000 (cancer); $90,000 (non-cancer) | Per-claim ceilings on noneconomic compensation for new Group B claims |
| Group B earnings calculation cap | $200,000 annual gross income | Cap used when calculating loss of earnings or employment benefits |
| State-sponsored terrorism payment limits | $20,000,000 per person; $35,000,000 per immediate family (for pro rata purposes) | Claim-size limits when dividing Fund payments; Iran embassy hostages (Nov. 4, 1979–Jan. 20, 1981) are eligible for $10,000 per day, and each eligible spouse or child for a $600,000 lump sum |

## Notable Sections

- **SEC. 402** reopens filing for five years after enactment (once regulations are updated), splits claims into Group A (award already issued) and Group B (new), and limits Group B eligibility to a WTC-related **physical** health condition. Mental health conditions are excluded, and economic loss covers past out-of-pocket medical expenses but not future medical expenses. The Special Master must issue policies within 30 days and update regulations within 180 days, and must prioritize the most debilitating conditions so spending stays within deposits to the Fund.
- **SEC. 402(g)** uses higher H-1B and L-1 fees as a pay-for, but dedicates the dedicated account to DHS’s biometric entry-exit system, not to victim payments, and only until $1 billion has been deposited.
- **SEC. 403** exempts the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund, the new Victims Compensation Fund, the United States Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund, and the World Trade Center Health Program Fund from sequestration.
- **SEC. 404** creates a Justice Department–administered fund for U.S. persons with final judgments against state sponsors of terrorism and for specified Iran hostage-crisis claimants. Payments are pro rata, attorneys’ fees are capped at 25% (with a criminal penalty for exceeding that), the United States is subrogated to paid claims, and new obligations from the Fund stop on January 2, 2026. The Fund is also fed by specified criminal and civil forfeiture proceeds tied to state sponsors of terrorism.
- **SEC. 405** bars the government from using BNP Paribas settlement funds for the Justice Department’s May 1, 2015 victim-compensation proposal, or for any terrorism-victim program except as this title directs, and rescinds $3.8 billion of those funds.

## Plain English

This title puts billions of dollars back into compensation for people made ill by the 9/11 attacks and cleanup, and sets up a separate fund to pay Americans harmed by state-sponsored terrorism, while capping many new awards and offsetting part of the cost with higher visa fees and a bank-settlement rescission.

## Title Summary

Title V amends Medicare and Medicaid payment rules under the Social Security Act. It cuts the balance of the Medicare Improvement Fund, reduces Medicare payments for film and computed-radiography X-rays to push providers toward digital radiography, eases the multiple-imaging professional-component discount, caps federal Medicaid matching for durable medical equipment (DME) at Medicare rates, and creates a separate Medicare home-health payment for certain disposable wound-therapy devices.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Medicare Improvement Fund (sec. 1898(b)(1)) | Reduced from $205,000,000 to $5,000,000 | Shrinks the fund available for Medicare program improvements |
| Film X-ray technical component (physician fee schedule and hospital outpatient) | 20% payment cut, 2017 and after | Discourages traditional film imaging |
| Computed radiography technical component | 7% cut (2018–2022); 10% cut (2023 and after) | Phased reduction for cassette-based digital imaging |
| Professional component of multiple imaging services | Multiple-procedure discount cut from 25% to 5%, beginning Jan. 1, 2017 | Increases payment relative to the prior discount; exempt from budget neutrality |
| Medicaid DME federal match | No new appropriation; federal share limited to Medicare fee-for-service (including competitive bidding) rates for items furnished on or after Jan. 1, 2019 | Caps what the federal government will match above Medicare rates |
| Applicable disposable devices (negative-pressure wound therapy) | Separate payment equal to the OPPS Level I HCPCS amount; Medicare pays 80% of the lesser of actual charge or that amount, items furnished on or after Jan. 1, 2017 | Pays home health agencies separately for specified disposable wound devices used instead of DME |

No other dollar appropriations appear in this title. Imaging and DME changes are rate rules, not line-item funding.

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 501 — Medicare Improvement Fund.** Directly reduces the statutory fund amount from $205 million to $5 million, a large rescission of available balances.
- **Sec. 502 — Imaging payment incentive.** New payment penalties for film (20%) and computed radiography (7%, then 10%) under both the physician fee schedule and the hospital outpatient system, applied outside budget neutrality so the savings are not redistributed to other services. Also replaces the 25% multiple-imaging professional-component discount with a 5% discount and repeals a related provision of the Protecting Access to Medicare Act of 2014.
- **Sec. 503 — Medicaid DME cap.** Beginning January 1, 2019, federal Medicaid reimbursement for DME fee-schedule amounts cannot exceed what Medicare would pay in the aggregate by class of item, including competitive-bidding rates. States may still cover items Medicare does not pay for. HHS must publicly evaluate the impact.
- **Sec. 504 — Disposable devices.** Creates a new, separate home-health payment for integrated disposable negative-pressure wound therapy systems that substitute for covered DME, effective January 1, 2017. Requires two GAO studies (reports due 18 months and 4 years after enactment).

## Plain English

Medicare will pay less for older X-ray methods, pay a bit more when doctors read multiple images at once, limit how much the federal government matches state Medicaid spending on equipment such as wheelchairs and oxygen gear to Medicare’s rates, and start paying home health agencies separately for certain disposable wound-treatment devices—while nearly emptying a $205 million Medicare improvement fund down to $5 million.

## Title Summary

Title VI changes how Medicare pays hospitals in Puerto Rico. It does not appropriate a fixed sum. It revises the Social Security Act so inpatient payments use the full federal rate, and it extends Medicare electronic health record (EHR) incentive payments under the HITECH Act to Puerto Rico hospitals.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Sec. 601 — Medicare inpatient hospital payment rate | Not specified in the title | For discharges on or after January 1, 2016, sets the Puerto Rico percentage at 0% and the federal percentage at 100%, so Puerto Rico hospitals are paid the full federal inpatient rate instead of a Puerto Rico–federal blend. |
| Sec. 602 — Medicare HITECH/EHR payments | Not specified in the title | Makes subsection (d) Puerto Rico hospitals eligible for Medicare EHR incentive payments and related payment adjustments, with delayed year references. |

No dollar amounts appear in this title. These are changes to mandatory Medicare payment rules, not line-item appropriations.

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 601** ends the special blended inpatient rate. On or after January 1, 2016, the applicable Puerto Rico percentage is 0 percent and the applicable federal percentage is 100 percent.
- **Sec. 602** extends Medicare HITECH EHR payments to Puerto Rico hospitals and applies as if enacted in the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009. To account for delay, year references are treated as 5 years later for Puerto Rico hospitals (7 years later for the payment-adjustment rule in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(ix)).
- **Sec. 602(c)** lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services implement the amendments by program instruction or otherwise, notwithstanding any other provision of law.
- The title creates no new program and imposes no beneficiary restrictions. It aligns Puerto Rico hospital treatment with existing Medicare inpatient and EHR payment rules.

## Plain English

Puerto Rico hospitals are paid Medicare inpatient rates on the same full federal basis as other U.S. hospitals and can receive Medicare electronic-records incentive payments, on a later schedule than hospitals in the states.

**Title VII — Financial Services** does not appropriate operating funds for financial regulators. It is a policy title: it restricts Treasury’s handling of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac senior preferred stock, amends banking, insurance, derivatives, and consumer-finance statutes, bars the SEC from using any funds in the Act for certain disclosure rules, and extends one housing-assistance authority while ending another.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Hardest Hit Fund extension (obligation cap) | Not to exceed $2,000,000,000 | Treasury may extend Emergency Economic Stabilization Act authority through December 31, 2017, only for current participants in the Housing Finance Agency Innovation Fund for the Hardest Hit Housing Markets; obligations after the extension may not exceed this cap |
| SEC political-disclosure rulemaking | No funds may be used | None of the funds in any division of the Act may be used by the SEC to finalize, issue, or implement a rule, regulation, or order on disclosure of political contributions, contributions to tax-exempt organizations, or dues paid to trade associations |
| All other sections (Secs. 702–706, 708) | No dollar amount | Statutory limits and amendments only; the text appropriates no sums |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 702 — Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac stock.** Until at least January 1, 2018, the Treasury Secretary may not sell, transfer, relinquish, liquidate, divest, or otherwise dispose of senior preferred stock acquired under the Senior Preferred Stock Purchase Agreements unless a later law specifically directs that disposition. A sense of Congress says the Secretary should not dispose of that stock until Congress enacts legislation on the enterprises’ future, even after that date.
- **Sec. 704 — CFPB and FACA.** The Federal Advisory Committee Act is applied to each Consumer Financial Protection Bureau advisory committee and each subcommittee of such a committee.
- **Sec. 705 — Affiliate swap exception.** Rewrites the Commodity Exchange Act and Securities Exchange Act end-user exception so an affiliate may use it only under strict ownership, hedging, and risk-management conditions, and not if the affiliate is (among other entities) a swap dealer, bank holding company, insured depository institution, credit union, private fund, or supervised nonbank financial company.
- **Sec. 706 — Insurance policyholders.** Extends Bank Holding Company Act “source of strength” limits that protect state insurance regulation to certain insurance-company holding companies and affiliates, and restricts FDIC liens in Dodd-Frank orderly liquidation when the firm is an insurance company: the state insurance authority must be notified, and the lien is allowed only to secure repayment and only if it will not unduly impede liquidation, rehabilitation, or policyholder recovery.
- **Sec. 707 — SEC funding rider.** Blocks use of any funds in the Act for SEC rules requiring disclosure of political contributions, contributions to tax-exempt organizations, or trade-association dues.
- **Sec. 708.** Repeals the reporting requirement in section 21(h)(6) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
- **Sec. 709 — Housing programs.** Hardest Hit authority may run through December 31, 2017, subject to the $2 billion cap and the current-participant limit above. The Making Home Affordable initiative terminates December 31, 2016; Home Affordable Modification Program applications filed before that date are not cut off.

## Plain English

This title does not fund new financial-agency budgets; it freezes Treasury’s sale of its Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred stock pending further legislation, tightens rules for banks, insurers, and derivatives affiliates, stops the SEC from spending this Act’s money on political-spending disclosure rules, keeps up to $2 billion available for existing Hardest Hit Fund participants through 2017, and ends the Making Home Affordable program at the end of 2016.

## Title Summary

Title VIII reauthorizes the Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) under 54 U.S.C. § 200302, extending the dates in the fund’s revenue-deposit and related authority from September 30, 2015, to September 30, 2018. It does not appropriate a dollar amount. It also limits use of Interior land-acquisition funds for condemnation for fiscal years 2016–2018, with a permanent exception for certain Everglades acquisitions.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| LWCF reauthorization (54 U.S.C. § 200302(b) and (c)(1)) | No dollar amount in this title | Extends authority through September 30, 2018 (was September 30, 2015) |
| Condemnation restriction on land-acquisition funds | No dollar amount | Bars use of specified FY2016–FY2018 acquisition funds for declarations of taking or condemnation complaints without House and Senate Appropriations Committee approval, unless otherwise provided in Division G or a later Interior appropriations act |
| Everglades exception | No dollar amount | Exempts funds to implement the Everglades National Park Protection and Expansion Act of 1989, and federal assistance to Florida for Everglades restoration land acquisition |

This title changes dates and conditions; it does not set an LWCF appropriation. Spending levels would appear in the Interior appropriations division (Division G) or a later appropriations act, not here.

## Notable Sections

- **SEC. 801(a) — Reauthorization.** A three-year extension of LWCF authority, through September 30, 2018. It does not create a new program or mandate a spending level.
- **SEC. 801(b) — Prohibition on condemnation / eminent domain.** For FY2016–FY2018, funds appropriated for acquisition of lands or interests in lands (under Division G or a later Interior appropriations act, unless that act says otherwise) may not be used to file declarations of taking or complaints in condemnation without approval of the House and Senate Committees on Appropriations.
- **SEC. 801(c) — Everglades exception.** The condemnation restriction does not apply—and the exception is written as permanent (“Hereafter”)—to funds for the Everglades National Park Protection and Expansion Act of 1989 or for federal assistance to Florida to acquire land for Everglades restoration.

## Plain English

This title keeps the Land and Water Conservation Fund authorized for three more years and generally blocks federal land buyers from using condemnation for those years unless congressional appropriators approve, except for specified Everglades land purchases.

## Title Summary

Title IX enacts the National Oceans and Coastal Security Act. It authorizes the NOAA Administrator and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation to establish a tax-exempt National Oceans and Coastal Security Fund and to award grants for ocean, coastal, and Great Lakes research, observation, and coastal infrastructure. It does not appropriate a fixed dollar amount; it authorizes “such sums as are necessary” for fiscal years 2017, 2018, and 2019.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| National Oceans and Coastal Security Fund | Such sums as are necessary (FY 2017–2019) | Deposits of amounts appropriated or otherwise made available to carry out the title |
| Grants to coastal States and U.S. territories | From Fund deposits (no fixed dollar amount) | Activities consistent with the title; distribution may consider shoreline miles, coastal population density, and other factors |
| National grants for oceans, coasts, and Great Lakes | From Fund deposits (no fixed dollar amount) | Eligible uses under section 905, including baseline science, ocean observing, and coastal infrastructure, coordinated with Federal and State agencies |
| Administrative expenses | No more than 2% of amounts deposited each fiscal year | Split between the Administrator and the Foundation under a documented agreement |

No specific dollar figures appear in the title text.

## Notable Sections

- **New program (sec. 904):** Creates the National Oceans and Coastal Security Fund and bars deposits of donations from foreign governments.
- **Use restrictions (sec. 905):** Funds may not be used to litigate against the Federal Government, or to fund creation of national marine monuments, marine protected areas, marine spatial planning, or the National Ocean Policy.
- **Grant design (sec. 906):** Requires procedures within 90 days of funds becoming available for administration; prioritizes cost-sharing by non-Federal partners; requires consultation with NOAA and the Interior Secretary; conditions State grants on Indian tribes being eligible for competitive grants; allows an advisory panel of industry, regional, and academic representatives; and requires a public online list of funded projects.
- **Oversight (secs. 904 and 907):** The Administrator may recover Federal payments after notice and a hearing if spending or procedures are noncompliant. Beginning with FY 2017, the Foundation must report annually to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Natural Resources Committee.
- **Authorization only (sec. 908):** Authorizes appropriations for FY 2017–2019 without specifying amounts. Certain National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Establishment Act provisions do not apply to amounts received under this title.

## Plain English

This title sets up a NOAA-linked fund so coastal states, tribes, local governments, nonprofits, and researchers can get grants to study and use oceans, coasts, and the Great Lakes, but it does not lock in a dollar amount and bars using the money for lawsuits against the Federal Government or for certain ocean-policy and protected-area activities.

## Title Summary

Title X sets budget-scorekeeping and allocation rules for Division M and later divisions of this Act. It does not appropriate funds to any agency, bureau, or program. It exempts those divisions from Statutory PAYGO and Senate PAYGO scorecards, limits how their costs are classified under discretionary spending limits, lets the House Budget Committee chair adjust FY 2016 allocations to match the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, and amends how CBO and OMB estimates are used under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| — | No dollar amounts in this title | Procedural budget rules only; no agency or program funding |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 1001 (Budgetary effects):** Keeps the costs of Division M and each succeeding division off both Statutory PAYGO scorecards (Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010) and Senate PAYGO scorecards (S. Con. Res. 21, 110th Congress). It also directs that those effects not be estimated for discretionary spending limits under section 251 of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, and not be treated as part of an appropriation Act for PAYGO classification. That is a scorekeeping exemption, not a spending cut or increase stated in dollars.
- **Sec. 1002 (FY 2016 allocation adjustment):** After enactment, the chair of the House Budget Committee may revise allocations, aggregates, and levels under S. Con. Res. 11 (114th Congress) so they match the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015. Adopted as an exercise of the House’s rulemaking power, which the House may change later.
- **Sec. 1003 (Estimates):** Amends 2 U.S.C. 901(a)(7)(B) so the relevant estimate language refers to both the CBO and OMB estimates of discretionary new budget authority, replacing language that cited the CBO estimate of the legislation and an OMB estimate of discretionary new budget authority and outlays.

## Plain English

This title does not fund programs; it changes how later parts of the bill are counted in Congress’s budget rules so those costs are not recorded on PAYGO scorecards or treated as ordinary appropriations for certain limit calculations.

## Title Summary

Title XI authorizes direct loans to Iraq in fiscal year 2016 under section 23 of the Arms Export Control Act, with gross obligations for principal capped at $2,700,000,000. It does not appropriate that sum as a grant; subsidy costs may be paid from Foreign Military Financing (FMF) funds already appropriated for Iraq and designated for Overseas Contingency Operations/Global War on Terrorism. The loans are for defense articles and services, with repayment due within 12 years.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Direct loan principal authority (AECA §23) | Up to $2,700,000,000 in gross obligations | Ceiling on principal of direct loans to Iraq in FY2016 |
| Budgetary cost of the loans (subsidy, including modifications) | No new dollar amount set; drawn from FMF Program funds in title VIII of the FY2016 State/Foreign Operations Act that are OCO/GWOT-designated and not reserved for countries other than Iraq | Cover the cost of making the loans, as defined in section 502 of the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 |
| Cost of selling, reducing, or cancelling amounts Iraq owes the United States | Included in the same cost authority; no separate amount stated | May be treated as part of loan costs |
| Borrower fees | Amount not specified; charged to borrowers under Congressional Budget Act §502(7) | Fees the U.S. Government may collect; may not be paid with funds made available to Iraq in the FY2016 Act or prior appropriations Acts |

## Notable Sections

- **Loan terms:** Repayment in not more than 12 years, including a grace period of up to 1 year on principal.
- **Country earmark protection:** Cost funding may not come from amounts specifically designated for countries other than Iraq.
- **Fee bar:** No FY2016 or prior State/Foreign Operations funds made available to Iraq may be used to pay fees on these loans.
- **End-use controls:** Section 3 of the Arms Export Control Act restrictions on transfer, retransfer, and end use apply to items bought with the loans.
- **Covered groups:** In consultation with the Government of Iraq, special emphasis must be placed on assistance to “covered groups” as defined in section 1223(e)(2)(D) of Public Law 114–92.
- **Congressional oversight:** Funds are subject to prior consultation with the appropriate congressional committees and to the regular notification procedures of the Committees on Appropriations.
- **Scorekeeping carve-out:** Section 1001 of title X of this division does not apply to this section.

## Plain English

In fiscal year 2016, the United States could lend Iraq up to $2.7 billion to buy U.S. defense articles and services, to be repaid within 12 years, with Congress notified before the money was used.
